title: Compile-Time Metaprogramming in CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: Activation Function Fusion: Generate specialized kernels for each activation function.
Precision Selection: Compile-time selection of compute precision (e.g., fp16, fp32).
Tile Size Specialization: Optimize kernels for specific tile sizes.
Feature Toggles: Enable/disable features at compile time.
Architecture-Specific Dispatch: Generate code optimized for specific GPU architectures.
constraints: Value of cutlass.Constexpr must be known at compile time.
Each configuration results in a separate kernel, increasing code size.
Avoid using compile-time parameters for frequently changing or data-dependent values.
compressed_summary: Compile-time metaprogramming in CuTe DSL enables the generation of specialized GPU kernels based on compile-time parameters, allowing for zero-overhead abstractions and optimized performance. The core concept involves using `cutlass.Constexpr` to mark parameters as compile-time constants, enabling decisions to be made during JIT compilation rather than at runtime. This approach eliminates runtime branching and allows for dead code elimination, resulting in smaller, more efficient kernels. Key patterns include Activation Function Fusion, where kernels are specialized for different activation functions, and Precision Selection, which allows for compile-time selection of compute precision such as fp16 or fp32. Tile Size Specialization optimizes kernels for specific tile sizes, while Feature Toggles enable or disable features at compile time. Architecture-Specific Dispatch generates code optimized for specific GPU architectures. Constraints include the requirement that `cutlass.Constexpr` values must be known at compile time and that more configurations lead to increased compilation time and code size. Best practices involve using compile-time parameters for configuration while keeping runtime parameters for data-dependent decisions. Metaprogramming in CuTe DSL is best suited for performance-critical decisions where the configuration is fixed or known at kernel launch time.
